findings.passage: One of my favorite things about South Dakota is how free we are – especially when it comes to the freedom to keep and bear arms. We have taken greater actions to defend our Second Amendment rights than any other state. As long as I am governor, I will continue to defend this basic constitutional freedom.
findings.note: Statement in his press release at the signing of three gun bills, as quoted by SDPB. The bills let permit holders keep pistols in vehicles in school lots, let city and county employees carry at work (and repeal the bar ban), and allow enhanced-permit holders to carry on college campuses.
subjects: carry a gun without a permit
guns on campuses and in bars

findings.passage: South Dakota also became the first state in the nation that doesn't charge a nickel for you to exercise your Second Amendment rights in obtaining a concealed carry permit if you choose to do so,
findings.note: Quoted by Dakota News Now at the suppressor bill signing. He says the state charges nothing for a concealed carry permit and that, as a legislator, he carried several bills supporting the Second Amendment.

findings.passage: South Dakota is the most Second Amendment-friendly state in the nation! We will keep it that way by cutting red tape and making sure companies know that we are Open for Opportunity. I’m currently working with legislators to deregulate suppressors at the state level.
findings.note: Written answer in an industry-group Q&A: says he is working with legislators to deregulate suppressors at the state level.

findings.passage: South Dakota is the freest state in a nation founded on the principle of freedom, and the Second Amendment exists to protect all our other rights.
findings.note: General statement on the Second Amendment from the same written Q&A.

findings.passage: In a letter to Trump and Attorney General Pam Bondi, Rhoden called the waiting period “unnecessary” now that background checks are federally required.
findings.note: News story's description of his letter; only the word 'unnecessary' is his quoted wording. The letter asks the federal government to drop the seven-day waiting period before shipping firearms and accessories (27 CFR 478.96), citing the effect on a Sioux Falls suppressor maker.
